newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Rate rise not enough to stem punt's fall-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Rate rise not enough to stem punt's fall-analysts.

text.p: Ireland's central bank sent a shot across currency speculators bows on Thursday with its surprise interest rate rise but economists said the rise alone would not be enough to stem the punt's fall.
Economists said the move was seen as more a statement of intent by the bank that it was not going to sit back and watch the punt go into freefall.
"The central bank's credibilily required them to do this," Dan McLaughlin, economist at Riada Stockbrokers, told Reuters. "They could not sit back and let the currency fall like a stone."
The bank raised the short-term facility rate to 6.75 percent from 6.25 percent on Thursday.

The move came in the wake of a sharp sell-off in the Irish currency since Wednesday morning on the expectation that the Irish authorities wanted the punt to enter a single currency in 1999 at close to the central European exchange rate mechanism. This would mean the currency needed to drop to in or around 2.41 marks.

"I think putting a floor under the currency is quite important for the central bank," AIB Capital Markets economist Pat O'Sullivan said. "No-one wants to see the cross fall so dramatically and they (the central bank) were particularly concerned about the fall from 0.9500 stg to 0.9100 stg because of the inflationary consequences."
"The move was basically driven by the need to cap inflation," O'Sullivan said.

Economists said the stronger-than-expected March Irish private sector credit growth, which showed rise of 18.6 percent in March from 15.8 percent in February, also added to the bank's inflation fears.
"Quite clearly if credit growth is growing at 18 percent plus it shows the economy is not slowing down," McLaughlin said.

He said the government's tax cuts introduced in its 1997 annual budget would also be feeding into the economy around now "... and the central bank probably feels we are already taking a lot of risks with inflation and the currency drop was the final straw."
McLaughlin said the authorities should have tightened rates last year and should not have had an expansionary budget which he said compounded the problem.

"I think if we are serious about EMU then we should have had a much tighter fiscal policy. Instead we had a loose fiscal policy and that meant exchange rates had to remain firm or interest rates had to go up or at least not come down," he said. "Instead what has happened is that the exchange rate has fallen."
Economists said if interbank rates continue to trade above the official STF rate the central bank may raise rates a second time.

"In 1995, in similar circumstances the central bank raised the STF by half a point in one week and another half a point the next," McLaughlin said. "Obviously this (rate rise) is done mainly to tighten domestic policy and we should see a half point rise in mortgage rates."
"But I don't think this is the end if cash rates stay above the STF."
Economists said the STF was considered a 'penal' rate at which the central bank lends money to banks.

"It is supposed to be a penal rate but effectively, due to the pressure of the falling punt, one month money was pushed up to 6.75 percent so banks could borrow money from the central bank at 6.25 percent and lend to each other at higher rates. This makes a nonsense of the whole thing," one economist said.
One month money was trading at 6.75/7.00 percent at the close of business on Thursday.
"People will wait to see how one month money settles. If it stays well above the STF then we can anticipate another rate hike with the knock-on impact on retail rates," McLaughlin said.
